Any Investor cards not dealt to the players are set aside for now. The Influence Card deck is shuffled and each player is dealt five cards face down. The player whose Investor is first in alphabetical order goes first. The player to the starting player’s right places the Dollar marker on any space on the game board. Each space on the game board represents a potential deal which Investors have to approve the deal and the number of dividends to be paid to those investors. On one’s turn, a player can open negotiations on the deal where the Dollar marker rests or roll the six-sided die. If the player rolls the die, the Dollar marker is advanced clockwise around the game board counting the available deals as spaces. Once the Dollar marker rests, the player may try to negotiate that deal or draw three Influence cards. If by drawing cards, the player’s hand exceeds twelve the player chooses which cards to discard to the limit. Should a player choose to make the deal, the player negotiates with the player or players representing the Investors how to divide the money at stake. The amount is number of dividends written on the space multiplied by value of the shares written on the deal tile. Any or all of the players may use their Influence cards to affect the outcome of the deal: Clan cards may act in place of Investors whether the Investors are in play or not. Travel cards put Investors out of play for the negotiations. Some are specific for a given Investor; some are wild to be played on any Investor. Recruitment cards can only be played in sets of three to steal another player’s Investor and make it your own. Boss cards give the player control of the negotiations. Stop cards immediately stop the effects of Travel, Recruitment, and Boss Influence cards The players are paid from the bank when a deal has been struck. The game board space is covered with the Deal tile (effectively closing the space from further game play), the Dollar marker is moved to the next open space, and play continues with next player. Once nine deals have been made, a die is rolled after each subsequent deal to determine whether the game ends (with the odds increasing each time). Victory goes to whoever has the biggest bankroll! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Overview A negotiation game in which a group of players compete and cooperate to put together profitable business deals. The goal is to make the most money. Components 98 Influence cards 15 Deal cards 6 Investor cards Dollar marker ​ Money Board Rules The money is sorted into denominations. Each player is randomly issued investor cards (usually one), with remainders placed face up near the board. The player with the first investor alphabetically will play first; the player to their right chooses which board space to place the dollar marker upon. The deck is shuffled and each player is dealt five cards. The tiles are sorted in order and placed on the board. Players act in turn. On each game turn, the acting player may either leave the marker in place or roll the die and advance the marker. If they do the latter, they may either play the new space or draw three cards from the deck. If a player does not draw cards, they may attempt to make a deal based on the current board position. Notations on the board dictate which investors must be involved to close the deal, as well as the number of shares that will pay out. The tile indicates the share price. Most spaces offer choices as to which investors to involve, while some do not. In order for a deal to occur, players who control the required investors must agree to the terms proposed by the acting player. Terms may only specify which investors will be involved and how the total proceeds of the deal will be distributed: no other offer of consideration is legal play. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Excellent.  A game I really don't like. I cannot believe how bad I thought (I know others like it but...)this game was. To make it worse is it in a big box - how many boxes of Fluxx can you fit in there.  I am still in a state of shock.  So glad I have played it though cos I don't have to play it again.  I won't either. I'm glad we all like different games - I'd hate to like this one.

[Rating: 1/10] As is, I consider the game broken and unplayable.  The Permanent Investors make it so that it's always in your interest to offer to accept the LOWEST amount possible as long as you are included in a deal, because you don't lose anything and at least you're getting some money instead of none.  I think if you took away the Permanent Investors and reworked some other ideas you could have a nice game.

[Rating: 1/10] This game was extremely popular when it was first released.  Basically the last person to make a trade wins the game.  There is no planning, no decision-making.  Just a lot of swapping cards with no purpose.  Its like Pit without the Chaos.

[Rating: 1/10] A popular party game from the old days - Heavily focused on negotiation, which may not appeal to everyone - Feels too outdated to stand out among modern board games

[Rating: 2/10] A dreadful negotiation game that is so random and devoid of structure as to be pointless. Good for the old "Junta" crowd, but if you like Chinatown, Bohnanza, Traders of Genoa, or the White Lotus, it'll be pretty painful to have to go back to this.

[Rating: 2/10] A negotiation game that is wildly chaotic and simply not that much fun. The "take that" card system feels decidedly at odds with the design's dealmaking core, and makes it difficult to bring any leverage into a discussion. Combined with the random end determination, the game devolves into the distinctly unpleasant experience of backing into any and all deals possible, if you're allowed, and usually for scraps.

[Rating: 2/10] Embarrased to say that the strategy required to win this game is beyond my abilities. My rating of the game reflects my desire to play again (which is slight) rather than the actual design or mechanics or game play. Just too many negotiation strategies for easy play, and agonizing decision on when to open a deal. A minor semantics complaint: The text (on the board itself) that listed the combinations of investors was hard to read from a distance. This game is just not my style. For some reason I like Diplomacy much more than this one.

[Rating: 2/10] Not a game for my taste. Too hectic, without real decisions to be made. Agonizing ebb and flow of "Bidding & Shouting"-battles and long periods of stupid card collecting. Don´t understand the fame it got...

[Rating: 2/10] Negotiation games are not my thing, and that's all this game is.  There's not even really any depth to the negotiations, it's just bang-bang-bang, who can talk the fastest.

[Rating: 2/10] I don't mind negotiation games per se (I enjoyed Chinatown, and I enjoy most trading games), but this game seems to deliberately be designed to destroy any sense of control or planning one may have.  Unenjoyable in the extreme.

[Rating: 2/10] An awful negotiation game.  There really isn't anything to negotiate - except to cause the perceived leader to fall back.  Couple this with random cards that destroy whatever negotiation you've already done, I couldn't wait for the game to end. Definitely will never play again, in this life or the next

[Rating: 2/10] A negotiation game with endless interruptions?  Ugh.  God, do I hate this game.  Everything that is brilliant about other negotiation games (Intrigue, e.g.) - breakable promises, the reliance on others for victory, temporary alliances, etc. - is missing here.   And as much as I dislike this Sackson "classic", it gets ten times worse when people even come close to taking it seriously:  "You're all ganging up on me!"  "You won't let me play cards!"  "I can't win!"  Sweet lord - someone kill me.

[Rating: 2/10] too many 'screw you' cards in circulation that get in the way of this being any good at all
